name: Mass gainer powders

lead: Mass gainers help hard gainers eat enough to gain size and muscle by adding a large number of calories in a drinkable form. According to Grokipedia, typical servings supply 500 to 1,500 calories, with a protein-to-carbohydrate ratio of around 1:2 or more.

The mechanism is a caloric surplus: gaining weight requires eating more energy than you use, and resistance training directs part of the gain toward muscle. A powder, often built on whey and maltodextrin, is a convenient energy-dense way to add calories. Evidence for mass gainers as a product category is limited, and forum users disagree on whether they are useful or whole food is preferable.

paras: People blend a scoop or two with milk or water, often as an extra shake between meals or after training, alongside lifting. Some use it for a bulk phase and stop when they reach their target weight.

In the US, supplements are regulated as foods and manufacturers confirm product safety themselves. A review of FDA data found muscle-building products among those contaminated with undeclared anabolic steroids, and a 2025 case report links a weight-gain supplement thought to contain steroids to pancreatitis with panniculitis. Users also report digestive complaints and acne in forums.

angle.text: Hard gainers use these calorie-dense shakes to eat enough for a surplus, which with training adds weight and muscle. They reliably add calories, and the evidence concerns overall energy intake rather than the powder itself.

lead: A mass gainer, or weight gainer, is a high-calorie powder supplement designed to help people gain weight and muscle by supplying a large amount of energy, mostly from carbohydrate with moderate protein and some fat, in a drinkable form [1].

Mass gainers are discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities by "hardgainers" and by people bulking. Some lifters regard them as a convenient way to hit calorie targets; others in the same forums argue that whole foods or plain protein are preferable [2].

Evidence specific to mass gainers as a product category is limited. The underlying principle, that weight gain requires a caloric surplus, is general nutrition; published case reports describe harms from products adulterated with steroids [3].
infobox: Carbohydrate (often maltodextrin), whey protein, fats, vitamins and minerals [1]

paras: Grokipedia describes mass gainers as combining whey protein concentrate, rapidly absorbed carbohydrate such as maltodextrin, and fats, sometimes with added vitamins, minerals, amino acids and digestive enzymes [1]. They differ from whey isolate products, which focus on protein with fewer calories [1].

Grokipedia traces calorie-dense muscle-building products to late 19th-century items such as Bovril and Plasmon, and says homemade high-calorie shakes were promoted to bodybuilders in the 1970s and 1980s, with commercial products from firms such as Weider and Optimum Nutrition following [1]. The article states online retail in the 2000s widened availability. These historical claims come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and have not been independently verified here.

In the US, DSHEA (1994) treats supplements as foods; manufacturers need no pre-approval and the FDA generally acts after a problem arises [4]. A study of supplements sold from 2007 to 2016 found 776 products with undeclared pharmaceuticals, and muscle-building products were contaminated with anabolic steroids [4]. Consumer Reports has reported heavy metals in several protein powders, and "protein spiking" allegations have been reported, which some companies disputed [4].

A 2025 case report in the Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences describes life-threatening pancreatitis with panniculitis associated with a weight-gain supplement; the report notes that mass gainers containing anabolic steroids have been linked in the literature to acute pancreatitis [3].

No clinical trials of mass gainer powders as a product have been found. A registered trial of overfeeding combined with resistance training in 32 participants (started 2019) examined body composition changes under a calorie surplus, and is about overfeeding generally rather than a commercial gainer [5]. Related research on whey protein reports moderate evidence that whey is a safe and effective add-on to training, though reviews disagree on whether high protein intakes meaningfully raise muscle mass [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mass gainers come up in discussions of bulking and supplements, with users split on whether they are useful [2].

claims.claim: Mass gainers harm gut health and may cause acne, so whole food is better.
Carbs and calories matter more than large amounts of protein for gaining.

timeline.event: DSHEA places dietary supplements in the US under food-style regulation [4].
Case report links a weight-gain supplement to pancreatitis with panniculitis [3].
